content.title: About
content.content: Bread with zucchini is a whole‑grain loaf that incorporates grated zucchini into the dough. The vegetable adds moisture, a subtle flavor, and boosts the nutritional profile with vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Zucchini is one of the lowest‑calorie vegetables, containing over 90 % water.
Adding zucchini to dough improves crumb softness and aroma.
Bread with zucchini is traditional in Mediterranean cuisine, where the squash is used in many summer dishes.
Zucchini is rich in vitamin C, which partially degrades during baking but some remains.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Zucchini provides vitamin C, supporting the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: The added zucchini contributes soluble and insoluble fiber, aiding digestion and satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Because of its high water content, the loaf remains relatively low‑calorie compared with regular white bread.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients in zucchini, such as lutein, have antioxidant effects.

items.title: Allergy to cucurbit vegetables
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to zucchini.

items.title: Glucosinolates content
items.content: Raw zucchini contains glucosinolates that can irritate the stomach in large amounts; baking destroys most of these compounds.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the bread is made with added salt, monitor intake, especially for individuals with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread with zucchini works well for breakfast, as a sandwich base, or alongside soups and salads. It can be toasted and topped with olive oil, avocado, or your favorite spread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the loaf in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Low‑fat cottage cheese is a dairy product made from skimmed milk by curdling and draining the whey. It has a soft, slightly grainy texture, a mild taste, and a low fat content (usually 0.5–2 %). Cottage cheese is widely used in diet nutrition and cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cottage cheese is one of the oldest dairy foods, known already in ancient Egypt.
Low‑fat cottage cheese is popular among athletes because of its high protein and low calorie profile.
The product is called cottage cheese in the US, творог in Russia, and twaróg in Poland.
Cottage cheese can be dry‑curd or contain a small amount of moisture; dry curd is easier to store and use in baking.
It is a common ingredient in traditional dishes such as pierogi, cheese pancakes, and casseroles.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Low‑fat cottage cheese provides about 12–14 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance and satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Its low fat content makes it suitable for calorie‑restricted and low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cottage cheese supplies calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Lactose levels are low, making it more tolerable for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein or whey proteins present in cottage cheese.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain low‑fat varieties are salted; choose unsalted versions if you need to limit sodium.

items.title: Shelf‑life control
items.content: Cottage cheese spoils quickly; discard it if it develops a sour smell or off‑color.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cottage cheese can be eaten plain, mixed into smoothies, salads, casseroles, pierogi, cheese pancakes, or used as a filling for crepes. It is often combined with berries, honey, or herbs for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cottage cheese in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C. It stays fresh for 5–7 days after opening. It can be frozen, though the texture may become more grainy.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork enchilada is a classic Mexican dish consisting of corn tortillas filled with seasoned shredded pork, smothered in a chili sauce and baked with cheese. It offers a rich, slightly spicy flavor complemented by cumin, oregano, and garlic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “enchilada” comes from the Spanish “enchilar,” meaning “to coat with chili sauce.”
Mexico boasts many regional variations, from red sauces made with dried chilies to green tomatillo‑based versions.
Traditional tortillas are made from masa (corn flour), though some regions use wheat flour.
Pork is often marinated in lime juice and spices before cooking, which tenderizes the meat.
The dish is commonly served with rice, beans, and fresh salsa on the side.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Pork provides complete animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Iron from pork supports normal hemoglobin levels and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: B‑vitamins, especially B12 and niacin, aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Moderate amounts of monounsaturated fats in pork can be heart‑friendly when consumed in balance.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Cumin, oregano, and garlic contain antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Large portions of pork may raise cholesterol levels, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked pork can harbor pathogens such as Salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to chili, cumin, or garlic.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauces and cheese add salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pork enchilada hot, topped with melted cheese, fresh cilantro, and a squeeze of lime. Pair it with rice, black beans, guacamole, or fresh salsa. Leftovers reheat well in the oven or microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked enchiladas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Moscow Mule is a cocktail made with vodka, ginger beer, and fresh lime juice, traditionally served in a copper mug. It originated in the United States in the early 1940s as a marketing effort to boost ginger beer sales and quickly became a bar classic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Moscow Mule was created in 1941 at the Cock ’n’ Bull bar in Los Angeles.
The name references Moscow, although the original recipe uses American vodka.
The iconic copper mug not only looks striking but also chills the drink rapidly, enhancing the ginger beer aroma.
Moscow Mule is often perceived as a “female” cocktail, yet it enjoys popularity across all demographics.
Since the 2020s, many variations have appeared: Gin Mule, Mexican Mule (with tequila), and a non‑alcoholic Virgin Mule.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Lime juice provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and offers antioxidant protection.

items.title: Ginger beer has anti‑inflammatory properties
items.content: Ginger is known for its anti‑inflammatory and digestive benefits, helping to ease nausea.

items.title: Moderate hydration
items.content: Because the majority of the drink is non‑alcoholic ginger beer, it can contribute to overall fluid intake.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Lime and ginger beer supply potassium, important for blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Moscow Mule contains vodka, so it should be consumed responsibly, especially by individuals with alcohol contraindications.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Commercial ginger beers often contain high amounts of sugar, which can be problematic for people with diabetes.

items.title: Ginger may irritate the stomach
items.content: In some individuals, ginger can cause heartburn or stomach irritation.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Lime may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the Moscow Mule in a chilled copper mug that has been pre‑cooled in the freezer. Combine 50 ml vodka, 15 ml fresh lime juice, and top up with ginger beer. Garnish with a sprig of mint or a lime wedge.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep opened ginger beer refrigerated and seal the bottle tightly. Store vodka in a cool, dark place. Clean copper mugs with a soft cloth, avoiding abrasive cleaners to preserve the finish.
